newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish coalition row could trigger early polls.
newsitem.headline: Polish coalition row could trigger early polls.

text.p: Poland could be headed for early parliamentary elections after the ex-communist group which dominates the coalition forced the dismissal of a cabinet minister belonging to its junior partner, the Peasant party.

The larger, ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party left its partner, the Polish Peasant Party (PSL), enraged when, without consultation, it forced the sacking of the Peasants' Foreign Trade Minister Jacek Buchacz on Wednesday.
Peasant leaders later quit a coalition meeting and said they would consult a forum of their own party on Friday before deciding what to do next.

The next formal coalition talks are unlikely until early next week and until then the future of the coalition and the date of the next elections, officially due late next year, are impossible to predict, ex-communist leader Jozef Oleksy said.
"I do not assume...that the coalition will fall apart, in fact I think it will survive, but no scenario can be ruled out today," Oleksy told Reuters.

If the coalition falls apart, bringing down the cabinet, President Aleksander Kwasniewski is likely to dissolve parliament, call early polls and appoint a temporary government, a source close to the presidential palace said.
The source, who asked not to be named, said the president would put the SLD, his own former party, in charge of the government, which would rule for several months.
Kwasniewski himself told reporters he hoped the coalition would last and that elections would be held late in 1997.
Buchacz's dismissal, over alleged irregularities in his ministry, was proposed by SLD Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz and promptly signed by Kwasniewski on Wednesday.

Despite Kwasniewski's and SLD's assurances to the contrary, many Peasant and opposition politicians said the minister's ousting was a provocation to force the Peasants to quit the coalition and bring about early polls.
There were signs it was working. "After such a humiliation, we might quit the government," Peasant deputy Aleksander Bentkowski was quoted as saying by Gazeta Wyborcza daily.
The coalition was created in 1993 after the parties, both rooted in the old communist system, heavily defeated groups derived from the former opposition to the old regime.
The alliance has survived policy clashes because the agrarian, pro-Church Peasants and the secular, pragmatic SLD have no alternative partners to ensure them a share of power.
Now that elections are approaching anyway, the arguments for the increasingly unnatural coalition are dwindling.
Some opposition analysts say the SLD wants early polls because its high opinion poll ratings may fall during coming tough debates on a cabinet reorganisation and on the budget.

"They (the SLD) may think it is better to have early polls than to enter extremely difficult talks with the Peasants on a new division of posts and on next year's budget," former foreign minister Andrzej Olechowski told Reuters.

After clearly leading for months, the SLD can now count on only 21 percent of the vote -- the same as a new opposition bloc led by the Solidarity trade union, a late August survey by public television's OBOP polling agency suggested.
The OBOP poll showed the Peasants with 10 percent -- partly explaining why the party is reluctant to face elections now.
PSL parliamentary leader Janusz Piechocinski suggested the SLD might want to bring down the coalition so as to shape next year's budget by itself to suit its own electoral interests.
"This would allow them to create a budget that makes their electorate -- pensioners, the police, the military and public sector workers -- feel things are improving," he said.
